Green sea urchins (Lytechinus variegatus) exhibit a complex life cycle that begins with the release of gametes during broadcast fertilisation events in shallow coastal waters. Following successful syngamy, the resulting embryos develop into free-swimming planktotrophic larvae that feed on phytoplankton. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the time after birth to the completion of larval metamorphosis, when the bilateral pluteus larva undergoes body plan reorganisation and settles onto the substratum, is approximately 56 days . During this pelagic period, the larvae graze on microalgae, accumulating the resources necessary for the development of the adult rudiment. The timing of settlement is critical, as it marks the transition to a benthic existence and the onset of the juvenile phase. These early life-history stages are particularly vulnerable to environmental variation, and the duration of the larval period can influence recruitment success in natural populations.

The transition from a planktonic existence to benthic life is followed by a period of rapid somatic growth in the juvenile stage. During this phase, individuals progress through sexual maturation, with the first signs of gonad development appearing under controlled thermal regimes. At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at which individuals attain puberty is estimated at 365 days [tp = 365 days]. This milestone is accompanied by a measurable increase in test diameter, with animals reaching a test diameter at puberty of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 28 grams [Wwp = approximately 28 grams], a value that reflects the substantial allocation of resources toward somatic growth prior to reproductive activation. This size threshold is consistent with patterns observed in other echinoids, where the onset of gametogenesis is tightly linked to the attainment of a minimum body size sufficient to support the energetic demands of spawning.

Reproductive output in Lytechinus variegatus has been estimated from fecundity data and spawning frequency observations under standard rearing conditions. At a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], females release approximately 13,425 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 13,425 eggs per day], representing a maximum reproductive rate that reflects the species' high fecundity. This daily output is partitioned into spawning events that occur periodically throughout the year. The energetic cost of such prolific gamete production is considerable and likely influences the trade-off between current reproductive effort and somatic maintenance. Field surveys indicate that spawning events are synchronized with periods of elevated phytoplankton abundance, ensuring that larvae encounter favorable feeding conditions upon hatching. The high fecundity of this species is typical of echinoderms that exhibit planktotrophic larval development, where only a small fraction of offspring survive to settlement.

The physical dimensions and body mass of adult Lytechinus variegatus have been documented from surveys of seagrass bed populations. The maximum recorded test diameter, or ultimate test diameter, reaches 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters], making this one of the larger species within its genus. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight attained by the largest adults is approximately 595 grams [Wwi = approximately 595 grams], a substantial mass that reflects the accumulation of gonadal tissue and skeletal carbonate over many years of growth. This asymptotic size is achieved only after several years of continuous feeding on seagrasses and associated epiphytes. Growth rates are influenced by local food availability and water temperature, with individuals in more productive habitats reaching larger sizes more rapidly. Comparisons with congeneric species suggest that the body size of L. variegatus is intermediate, falling between smaller Lytechinus species and the larger Echinometra species that share similar habitats.

Longevity in Lytechinus variegatus has been assessed through field studies and captive rearing experiments. At a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 5,840 days [am = approximately 5,840 days], equivalent to roughly 16 years under favorable conditions. This extended lifespan is characteristic of echinoids with slow somatic growth and deferred reproductive maturity, allowing individuals to accumulate reproductive output over many breeding seasons. The earliest life stages also exhibit a remarkably small initial mass, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.00000088 grams [Wwb = 0.00000088 grams], reflecting the microscopic size of the fertilized egg. This minute starting mass imposes a severe constraint on early development, requiring efficient yolk utilization during the embryonic period before the onset of planktotrophic feeding. As individuals age, growth rates decelerate markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity, consistent with the life-history pattern observed in many long-lived marine invertebrates.
